description: We are a group of passionate engineers from the University of Chicago.
summary:
BeforeTheSmoke is a web app that uses NASA and ISRO’s NISAR radar satellite to track rice harvests across Punjab, India, and their connection to crop burning. Every autumn, Punjab faces a serious air pollution crisis. Farmers have only a short window to clear rice straw before planting wheat, and thousands of fields are set on fire, sending smoke across entire communities and contributing to dangerously poor air quality. By November 11, 2026, approximately 5,500 farm fires had already been recorded across the state. We want to help change this by making it easier to understand where and when harvesting happens, and where alternatives to burning are needed most.

Our app follows 24 satellite passes across a 29 km region, tracking changes in radar signals to estimate when individual 100 m rice fields are harvested. We visualize these harvest dates as a wave of color across an interactive map, alongside NASA FIRMS fire detections. Users can follow a guided walkthrough of the growing season or explore individual fields and their radar histories. By making complex satellite data accessible to everyone, we hope to help officials and communities make better-informed decisions to reduce crop burning.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

In Punjab, farmers grow rice during the monsoon season and wheat through the winter. Between the two growing seasons, many fields are cleared by burning leftover rice straw. Our project, Before the Smoke, uses data from NISAR, a radar satellite built by NASA and ISRO, to track when and where rice fields are harvested.

When users open the site, they are taken through a ten-step walkthrough of a 29 km area in southern Tarn Taran district, stretching from Patti town to the Harike wetland. The walkthrough follows 24 radar passes over the course of the year, showing how fields change as they flood in June, fill with growing rice, and are harvested in October. We then bring in NASA's fire detections to show where fires were recorded and when they occurred.

After the walkthrough, users can explore the map on their own. They can play through the year, switch between the two radar views, turn fire detections on or off, and click on individual locations to see how their radar signals changed over time.

HOW IT WORKS

Unlike regular satellite cameras, radar sends out its own signal. This means it can collect data at night and through haze, which makes it useful for monitoring fields during periods when optical images may not be clear. Growing rice has a strong radar response, while a harvested field produces a much weaker one.

Our pipeline processes a small area from each NISAR data file, which can be nearly 7 GB in size. It reduces radar noise and tracks how the signal changes as fields go from flooded to fully grown. We use this pattern to identify rice fields, then look for a sharp drop in the signal between consecutive passes. Each 100 m rice cell is assigned to the pair of passes where that drop occurs, which gives us an estimate of when it was harvested. To reduce false detections, we only count drops above a threshold calibrated to a 2% false-alarm rate. We call the resulting map the Harvest Wave.

We also compare our results with other sources of data, rather than relying on radar alone. These include 452 fire detections from NASA FIRMS, optical imagery from Copernicus Sentinel-2, and official harvest reports.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

NISAR data can be difficult to work with without experience in remote sensing. We wanted to make it accessible to people who may not have that background, including local legislators, district officials, agricultural advisers, teachers, and reporters. Instead of having to download and process large satellite files, they can open a link and explore how fields changed throughout the year.

The site works in a browser on both phones and laptops, and does not require an account or login.

We also want to be careful about how we talk about crop burning. Farmers have a very short window to clear their fields and prepare for the next wheat season, so burning is not simply a matter of individual choice. We hope that making harvest patterns and fire detections easier to see can help farmers, officials, and others involved in planning discuss where equipment for managing leftover straw and other clean-air measures are most needed.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

We wanted to make a full year of satellite data easier to understand than a collection of radar images or technical charts. The site starts with a guided walkthrough, where users can follow the changes in the fields over time. On the map, the estimated harvest dates appear as a wave of color moving across the region.

The site also compares the radar-based harvest estimates with recorded fires and other sources of information. This helps users see where the different datasets support each other and where they do not. We show those differences rather than presenting our estimates as a perfect record of what happened.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

We put a lot of thought into making sure the site represents the data honestly. We do not fill in missing values or present estimates as confirmed observations. Six radar passes are missing, and the site shows them as missing along with the reasons. We also identify where data comes from two different releases so users can understand the source of what they are seeing.

There are limits to what our results can show. The satellite track we used revisits the area every 12 days, so we cannot determine the exact day a field was harvested. As of November 4, our map had identified harvest activity on about two thirds of the rice fields, compared with an official figure of 85% across the state. We make these limitations clear on the site so users can put the results in context.

We also considered accessibility and usability. The map colors were tested for color-blind accessibility, text contrast was checked in both light and dark modes, and interactive controls have visible focus indicators for keyboard users. The site is also mobile-friendly, so users can explore the map and its controls on a phone as well as a desktop.

TOOLS

Data: NISAR L2 GCOV from the Alaska Satellite Facility DAAC, NASA FIRMS (VIIRS), Copernicus Sentinel-2, and basemap data from OpenFreeMap and OpenStreetMap.

Pipeline: Python, NumPy, SciPy, h5py, rasterio, and earthaccess.

Web app: TypeScript, React, MapLibre GL, and geotiff.js. Built with Vite and tested with Vitest and Playwright.

Hosting: GitHub Pages. We do not run our own server; the app reads small portions of the satellite data files directly.

AI assistant: Claude through Claude Code, as described in our AI-use answer.

Hardware: Our own computers, with no specialized hardware.
